name: Quanta Don't Bleed (But We Do)
description:
Released in 2201 by the Gray Zone-born vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Osei Vantarín-Khoury, 'Quanta Don't Bleed (But We Do)' became the defining protest anthem of the Circuit Uprising — a wave of labor strikes and corporate resistance that swept through Tiers 1 and 2 between 2201 and 2203. The song opens with a lone kora line layered over a low industrial drone, before a wall of polyrhythmic percussion and distorted hurdy-gurdy crashes in at the chorus. Vantarín-Khoury's voice is raw and unprocessed — a deliberate aesthetic choice when polished vocal correction was universal — and the contrast became a political statement in itself. The title's grammatical bluntness was intentional: 'Quanta' as currency, as abstraction, as the thing that moves through the city's veins while workers bleed in its maintenance tunnels.

Vantablack Media subsidiary Crescent Conduit attempted to license a sanitized version for a corporate wellness campaign in 2204, stripping the bridge — which names three specific corporate executives responsible for the Tier 2 ventilation cuts of 2200 — and reframing it as motivational content. The backlash was immediate and severe. Vantarín-Khoury released a public neural-feed statement calling the attempt 'the most honest thing they've ever done.' The original remains on the gray market; the corporate version was pulled within a week and is now itself a collector's curiosity.
creator: Osei Vantarín-Khoury
audience: Tier 1 and Tier 2 workers, union organizers, labor activists, anti-corporate subcultures; widely known in Tier 3 but rarely played openly
cultural_impact: The song functioned as a kind of password during the Circuit Uprising — humming the kora line in a maintenance corridor was enough to identify a sympathizer. Corporate security flagged the melody pattern in audio surveillance systems, which only deepened its symbolic weight. It has been sung at every major labor funeral in the Gray Zone since 2201, and the line 'We built the Spire with borrowed lungs' is painted on at least forty walls across Tiers 1 and 2. Tier 5 residents are largely unaware of it, and that ignorance has itself become a cultural shorthand for discussing class division in GLMZ.
story_hooks: A corporate fixer is sent to locate Osei Vantarín-Khoury before the anniversary of the Circuit Uprising, when a planned mass public performance of the song threatens to reignite labor tensions — but the fixer grew up in the Gray Zone and knows every word.

A Tier 4 executive's teenage child has the song on a contraband data chip and is caught humming it in a Spire school — the family must decide whether to turn the child in or cover it up, and what that choice reveals about who they've become.
The Vantablack corporate version surfaces at a Tier 3 memorial service, accidentally played by a well-meaning event planner who didn't know the difference — and someone in the room does.
